content: Hey, good morning! I've been meaning to check in since things finally got moving on the ground. Construction officially kicked off on June 9, 2025 — watching Yamamoto-san's crew pull up in front of 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu with all their equipment was honestly a bit surreal. After all the permitting headaches, the material sourcing conversations, and months of loan paperwork, it's strange in the best possible way to see actual people in hard hats walking around inside the space. I went by yesterday afternoon and they'd already stripped out the old suspended ceiling and most of the partitions from the previous tenant. The bones look better than I expected, actually — the slab height is good, the structural columns are where the drawings said they'd be, and nothing alarming has appeared yet. I know we've talked through a lot of the design decisions over the past several sessions, but I want to use today to lock in the remaining material choices and also run a few things by you that came up in my meeting with the architect last week. There's one suggestion she made that I haven't fully decided on yet and I'd value an outside perspective.

That's a genuinely exciting milestone — June 9, 2025 is a date you'll probably remember for a long time, right alongside the day you signed the lease. There's something fundamentally different about seeing the physical space transform after months of working exclusively through documents, drawings, and spreadsheets. The fact that the slab height is good and the structural columns are where the drawings indicated is meaningful early news — those are the things that are hardest to compensate for if they're wrong, so finding them correct gives you a real foundation to build from.

I'm glad you want to use this session to firm up the outstanding decisions. Before we dive into the specifics, can you remind me where things stand on the overall construction timeline? Last we talked, Yamamoto-san had given you a rough target window but I want to make sure I'm working from the most current information. And what were the main open items that came out of your architect meeting — was it primarily the interior finishes you still needed to lock in, or were there layout and flow questions still on the table as well? I want to make sure we get through everything that needs a decision before any procurement deadlines hit.

Right, so on the timeline: Yamamoto-san confirmed the projected completion date is August 22. That gives us roughly ten weeks from the June 9 start, which he said is realistic provided we don't run into any significant surprises inside the walls. There's actually one section near the back kitchen wall where he suspects the previous tenant's fit-out may have included some non-standard plumbing routing — he said the way the existing fixtures were positioned suggests whoever did the original work may have run a branch line through an area that's going to need to be cleared before we can do our rough-in. So his team is going to open that wall cavity carefully this week and assess. If it's clean, we're fully on schedule for August 22. If there's real remediation work needed, we might need to add a week, but he was cautiously optimistic. He's seen worse.

On the architect meeting — the main open items were three things: the floor material, the wall treatment in the dining room, and then a layout suggestion that I haven't decided on yet and really want to talk through. The floor and wall choices I feel pretty settled on at this point, but the layout question has more moving parts and I want a second opinion before I give her a final answer.

August 22 as the projected completion is helpful to have clearly in mind — that gives you roughly five to six weeks of buffer before a realistic soft-open window if you're thinking late September or early October for your first guests. Ten weeks is tight for a full restaurant fit-out, but it's not uncommon in Tokyo when the scope is well-defined, the contractor has the right crew size, and materials procurement is running in parallel with construction rather than sequentially. The key is that nothing in the critical path slips.

The potential plumbing situation behind the kitchen wall is worth keeping close tabs on. Non-standard routing from a prior tenant either turns out to be minor — a branch line that can be capped without much drama — or it becomes a real schedule and budget event if the routing is extensive or if there is any associated moisture damage. It's good that Yamamoto-san spotted the signs before breaking ground on your rough-in. Do you have a contingency budget line for this kind of in-wall discovery, or is that still a conversation you need to have with him?

Let's work through the materials first since those are procurement-sensitive. The floor choice tends to have the longest lead time in most fit-outs, so I'd like to understand that one before anything else. What did you and the architect land on?

There is a contingency — we built about 800,000 yen in reserve specifically for in-wall surprises and unexpected structural conditions. Yamamoto-san knows to call me immediately if they find something that would push past that number, and we'll evaluate whether to draw from it or scope something differently. I feel reasonably protected there unless it's something genuinely catastrophic, which Yamamoto-san thinks is unlikely given the building's age and construction type.

For the floor, we've settled on white oak engineered plank. The architect's original concept was a more standard parquet pattern in a darker walnut stain, which I can see the logic of — it would have been grounded and classic — but I pushed back on it pretty hard after sitting with it for a few days. What I kept coming back to was that I want the space to feel light and genuinely Milanese, almost like you're dining in a well-appointed apartment in the Brera district rather than in a formal ristorante. The white oak achieves that warm-but-airy quality in a way the darker parquet just didn't. And from a practical standpoint, the engineered construction handles humidity fluctuation significantly better than solid hardwood, which matters a great deal given how Tokyo summers behave with the kitchen humidity load added on top of the seasonal ambient moisture.

The supplier the architect lined up is Toyo Wood Works — they're a specialty importer based out of Yokohama who focuses almost entirely on high-end hospitality and residential projects. Their lead time on the white oak engineered plank is six weeks from order confirmation, which aligns well with the August 22 completion target as long as we lock in the order this week. I've reviewed the spec sheet and I'm comfortable with the product. I just want to make sure I'm not missing anything before I pull the trigger.

The white oak engineered plank choice makes a great deal of sense for what you're describing, and I think your instinct to push back on the darker parquet was the right one. The Brera district reference is a useful north star for the entire space — that neighborhood tends to produce interiors that feel genuinely residential in their warmth and ease, neither rustic nor minimalist, with materials that have natural depth rather than applied drama. White oak achieves that register better than almost anything else you could put on the floor at a reasonable price point.

A few practical details worth confirming with Toyo Wood Works before you finalize the order: first, the plank width. Something in the 120 to 180 millimeter range would reinforce that relaxed, apartment-scale quality you're after; anything narrower starts to feel more traditional and strips some of the contemporary ease out of the aesthetic. Second, and more consequentially, the surface finish. There's a meaningful difference between an oil finish and a UV-lacquer finish both visually and in terms of ongoing maintenance. An oil finish reads more natural, responds more honestly to light, and — critically for a restaurant — allows for localized repair and recoating without having to refinish the entire floor surface. A lacquer finish is more durable initially but creates a plastic-looking sheen and requires full resanding when it eventually needs work. For a candlelit dining room, oil finish almost always wins on aesthetics.

The humidity argument for engineered over solid is absolutely correct for Tokyo. A solid hardwood floor in a restaurant kitchen adjacency, with steam load all summer and forced-dry heating in winter, is a real expansion-and-contraction problem. The cross-laminated core of the white oak engineered plank handles that dimensional movement significantly better and is far less likely to cup or gap over time. You made the right call there.

On Toyo Wood Works specifically — I'm not personally familiar with that importer, but their specialization in high-end hospitality work is a good signal. Six weeks from order confirmation to delivery is the critical variable, and I'd want written confirmation of that timeline, not just a verbal estimate, before you treat it as firm. Has the architect also specified the installation pattern — straight run parallel to the main window wall, or something angled or herringbone?

The finish question is a good one to flag — I need to follow up with Toyo Wood Works explicitly on that point because the spec sheet I was given listed it as 'natural oil finish' without more detail, and I want to confirm it's a hardener oil rather than a raw linseed or similar, because I've read that raw oil finishes in commercial settings can be slow to cure and susceptible to early marking. The architect recommended oil over lacquer for exactly the reasons you described, especially the spot-repair argument. A restaurant floor gets dragged chair legs, dropped wine glasses, and the occasional wheeled serving cart — knowing we can address a localized worn area without a full floor shutdown matters a lot operationally.

On the installation pattern: straight-run parallel to the main window wall. The architect's reasoning is that it visually elongates the dining room toward the garden view, which is one of the best spatial assets the space has. I walked through it with her last Tuesday and I agree completely — the window wall and the view beyond it are going to be a major selling point for the restaurant, and any design decision that draws the eye in that direction is the right call. We're also planning a subtle variation in the board lengths to avoid the too-regular look that sometimes makes engineered plank feel manufactured.

Now the wall treatment — this is honestly where I got most excited in the architect meeting. She introduced me to a product called Marmorino, which is a traditional Venetian polished plaster with a very long history in Italian interiors. We're specifying it as a limestone-finish plaster for the dining room walls specifically. The texture sits somewhere between fully matte and a very subtle eggshell-level sheen — it catches light differently depending on the viewing angle and the light source, which I think is going to be extraordinary with the candle and pendant lighting we've planned. The importer for Marmorino in Japan is Tokai Sangyo, and they distribute through their Nagoya center. Lead time on that is about three weeks, which is much more comfortable than the floor timing.

The hardener oil point is worth confirming before you finalize the Toyo Wood Works order — it's exactly the right thing to ask. In commercial settings, hardener-modified oils, sometimes called hard-wax oils, provide much better early durability and don't leave the floor vulnerable during the cure period the way a pure oil would. Danish Oil and products like Rubio Monocoat are well-known examples in the category. If Toyo Wood Works's factory finish is already a hard-wax oil applied under controlled conditions, that's actually preferable to a site-applied finish because the cure environment is more consistent. If the boards are arriving unfinished or with a raw oil, you'll want to discuss application timing with Yamamoto-san so the floor has adequate cure time before furniture moves in.

The variation in board lengths is a nice touch — it's the kind of detail that doesn't register consciously but makes a space feel less like it came out of a box. Combined with the straight-run direction pulling toward the garden view, the floor should function almost like architecture — it directs movement and gaze simultaneously.

The Marmorino and white oak engineered plank pairing is very coherent — both materials sit in the warm-neutral palette, both carry natural surface texture rather than applied decoration, and both age well. A restaurant with these finishes will look better in five years than on opening night. The limestone-finish plaster has depth and movement that only reveals itself in a real space with real light, and the layered illumination from your pendants and candles will reward it well.

A practical question: has the architect already identified a certified applicator for the Tokai Sangyo Marmorino product? Venetian plaster of this type is extremely technique-sensitive, and the burnishing stage in particular requires someone who has worked with this material before. An inexperienced plasterer with good general skills can still produce inconsistent results on Marmorino. Some importers maintain a registry of applicators who have been formally trained on their specific product line. It's worth asking Tokai Sangyo directly whether they can point you toward certified applicators in the Tokyo area.

The architect was ahead of you on that one, which made me very happy to hear. She's worked with Tokai Sangyo before on a boutique hotel project in Minami-Aoyama — she said the limestone-finish plaster on that project was one of the things guests commented on most consistently, which tells me she has real-world evidence that Marmorino delivers in practice, not just in theory. She already identified an applicator from Tokai Sangyo's recommended list who is Chiba-based and has completed around a dozen Marmorino installations over the past three years, including a couple of restaurant projects. We're meeting him next Tuesday for a site walkthrough. I asked the architect to have him bring samples at a minimum of two application densities so we can see how the limestone-finish plaster reads in the actual space under the actual window light rather than in a showroom. I've learned through this whole project that finishes behave completely differently depending on the specific orientation of the room, the quality of the light coming through the windows at different hours, and even the ceiling height. So I want to evaluate Marmorino in context before I make any final quantity decisions.

That brings me to the layout question, which is the one I've been going back and forth on. The architect's suggestion was that instead of the original plan — which was two separate small bathrooms, one labeled men's and one labeled women's — we shift to a single accessible unisex bathroom layout. Her argument has two main components. First, that a single well-finished accessible unisex unit is more inclusive and better aligned with the kind of contemporary European restaurant we're positioning this as. And second, the configuration change would recover approximately 3.2 square meters that we could use to extend the bar seating area, which is currently one of the tighter elements of the floor plan. The plumbing rough-in hasn't happened yet so there's still time to revise the drawings. I genuinely haven't made up my mind. What's your read?

This is a real decision worth thinking through carefully, and I think the architect is pointing you in a sound direction — though the reasoning behind it matters as much as the conclusion.

The single accessible unisex layout has become increasingly standard in upscale contemporary restaurant design over the past several years, particularly in European-concept restaurants where the positioning is built around intimacy, conviviality, and a certain residential ease rather than formal hierarchy. In a northern Italian restaurant aiming specifically for a Brera-apartment quality — warm, unhurried, a place where people feel like guests rather than customers — a single beautifully finished bathroom actually reinforces the concept better than two cramped divided rooms would. When guests encounter a thoughtfully designed single unisex facility, the implicit message is that the restaurant considered the entire experience, not just the parts that are visible from the dining room. When they encounter two narrow gender-segregated rooms that feel like an afterthought, that's a different message.

There's also a guest experience practical argument beyond the space recovery. Two small rooms in a tight footprint often end up being poorly ventilated, awkwardly arranged, and harder to keep clean during service. A single larger accessible unisex unit gives you room for proper fixtures, a proper vanity, good lighting, and a ventilation specification that actually works. The material language can also carry through from the dining room — if you use limestone-finish plaster or a related treatment in the bathroom, it becomes part of the spatial narrative of the restaurant rather than a separate utilitarian space.

The 3.2 square meters recovered is not trivial. In a 38-cover restaurant, that footprint could yield two to three additional bar seats, which at your anticipated cover average represents real incremental revenue per service. But the more important effect of bar seating at a northern Italian concept isn't seat count — it's atmosphere. Bar seats are where solo professionals eat on a Tuesday without feeling self-conscious, where regulars sit for a quick glass and a plate of something small, and where a good amount of the ambient energy of the dining room actually gets generated. The bar is often the social engine of a room even when it's not the largest revenue element.

The compliance question is important: you'll want your architect to confirm in writing that the single accessible unisex layout meets all current Tokyo Metropolitan Government requirements for commercial food service facilities. The Tokyo Barrier-Free Ordinance and the Building Standards Law have specific dimensional minimums and fixture requirements for accessible restroom facilities. Your architect almost certainly knows this, but getting her confirmation documented in the project file before the rough-in is the kind of verification that protects you during the final inspection. What's your instinct on how your target guests will experience the configuration?

My instinct is that it's going to be fine, actually better than fine for the kind of guests I'm hoping to attract. The people I'm imagining in this restaurant — they're the kind of guests who've had dinner at Arpège in Paris or spent an evening in a good osteria somewhere in the Navigli district in Milan, and they certainly didn't think twice about the bathroom configuration in those places. At the price point we're operating at and with the traveler-and-local mix I'm expecting, a single well-finished single accessible unisex bathroom reads as sophisticated and considered rather than inconvenient. If anything, the two small cramped separate rooms would feel more dated to that particular guest than the single unit would.

My main concern was always operational — specifically whether a single unit creates a bottleneck during peak service. At 38 covers during a busy Friday dinner, if there's a visible queue forming at one bathroom that's temporarily occupied, that's uncomfortable for the guests and for the floor staff. But I ran some rough calculations: at 38 covers with a typical dinner duration of about 100 minutes, assuming roughly one bathroom visit per guest over the course of the meal and some natural distribution across the service window, the utilization rate doesn't suggest a meaningful problem. The architect made essentially the same argument when I raised it with her, and she added that two small separate rooms with simultaneous occupancy creates a different version of the same problem — the queue still forms, it's just distributed between two doors instead of one. So in terms of the pure flow question, the difference is smaller than intuition suggests.

I'm landing on yes. I'll confirm with the architect that the single accessible unisex layout is compliant with all applicable municipal requirements as you mentioned — I want that confirmed in writing before the rough-in drawings are finalized — and then we'll proceed with the layout change. The remaining question is how to allocate the recovered 3.2 square meters between bar extension and other possible uses.

Your utilization reasoning is sound, and your point about the distributed queue being different rather than absent is a good one that's often underappreciated in these discussions. Two occupied single-gender rooms with people waiting at both doors is not meaningfully better from a guest experience standpoint than one occupied unisex room with one person waiting. The perception of the situation changes, but the arithmetic doesn't improve as much as the floor plan change might suggest.

On the allocation of the recovered 3.2 square meters: I want to gently push back on treating this as purely a bar extension decision, because there's a competing use that I think deserves real weight. Coat and bag storage near the entrance is one of those hospitality elements that guests in your target demographic notice acutely, even if they don't articulate it. In Tokyo's climate, guests arrive in the fall and winter wearing coats that don't fit over the back of a chair without sliding off, carrying bags they don't want on the floor, and sometimes with umbrellas that need somewhere to go. If the answer to all of that is essentially 'put it on the back of your chair and hope for the best,' the visual and experiential effect is real — a well-dressed dining room that should feel effortless starts to look cluttered. A built-in coat alcove near the entrance, even a modest one — perhaps a recessed panel with brushed brass hooks and a small shelf above, finished in the same material language as the rest of the entry — signals a quality of hospitality attention that guests who've been to Arpège or to a good Navigli osteria will recognize immediately.

If the 3.2 square meters can be intelligently split — something like two-thirds toward bar extension, one-third toward a dedicated coat recesses — that might produce a better overall outcome than maximizing bar seat count at the expense of the arrival experience. I'd bring this specific framing to your architect and see how she responds. She may have already considered it, or she may have a better spatial solution than a simple partition of the recovered area.

The compliance confirmation in writing before rough-in is absolutely the right approach for the single accessible unisex layout, and once you have it, I'd keep a copy alongside the relevant construction drawings in your project file rather than relying on it being somewhere in an email chain. Where are you in terms of overall procurement timing? Is the Toyo Wood Works order for the white oak engineered plank going in this week as planned, and is the Tokai Sangyo Marmorino order also being placed on a parallel track, or are you waiting for the Tuesday walkthrough before committing to that quantity?

The coat storage framing is exactly the kind of thing I should have been thinking about more explicitly, and I'm glad you raised it. You're right that it's not just a square meter allocation question — it's a first-impression question. The entrance from the street to the dining room is already one of the spatial transitions I've been thinking about most carefully, because the entrance corridor is narrow and I want guests to feel like they've crossed a meaningful threshold rather than just walked into a room. A dedicated coat area near the entrance, however modest, is part of making that transition feel intentional and hospitable rather than improvised. I'll put that to the architect specifically and ask her to model a split scenario before I commit to giving everything to the bar extension.

On procurement timing: the Toyo Wood Works order for the white oak engineered plank is going in this Friday. I've reviewed the spec sheet, confirmed the plank dimensions and the installation quantity with the architect, and the only thing I need to do before placing it is confirm the oil finish specification — which I'll do on a call with Toyo Wood Works tomorrow. Once that's confirmed, the order goes in Friday morning. Six weeks from confirmation puts delivery in late July, which gives Yamamoto-san's crew adequate time to acclimate the boards before installation ahead of August 22 completion.

The Tokai Sangyo order for the Marmorino plaster is on hold until after Tuesday's walkthrough with the applicator. He may have site-specific preparation requirements — humidity levels in the space at time of application, whether we need to run dehumidifiers beforehand, how many days of open time we need to build into the schedule around the plaster application sequence. Marmorino is mixed in batches and you genuinely cannot color-match a second order if you've underestimated the first one, so I would rather wait until I have the applicator's direct input before finalizing the quantity. That probably means the Tokai Sangyo order goes in Wednesday or Thursday of next week.

Overall I feel like we're in a genuinely solid place. The June 9, 2025 start is real, the team is on site, August 22 is achievable if the plumbing turns out to be clean, the materials decisions are largely made, and the one layout question I was uncertain about has resolved itself in the conversation. I think the next session I'll most need your help with is kitchen equipment installation sequencing, because that's the other piece with significant lead times that I want to make sure doesn't create a bottleneck in the back half of the construction schedule. Can we plan to cover that next time?
